title: kirtan repertoire (20 songs)
hook: the harmonium is ready, the room is full, and the first song goes to the god of beginnings
carry: the first obstacle is opening your mouth

segments.voice: This week we followed the Bhagavata's tenth book past the cowherd years: a teacher's fee, a princess's letter, a missing jewel, and yesterday a poor friend who never asked, a handful of rice, eaten with delight. Which scene would you tell first? Today the stories turn into songs. Day nine hundred eighty-seven.
screen: `THE BHAGAVATA'S TENTH BOOK.` · `PAST THE COWHERD YEARS.` · `NOW, THE SONGS.`

segments.voice: A rug on the floor, a harmonium in the middle of it, a pair of small hand cymbals waiting beside a drum. People drift in and sit cross-legged. Some know every word. Some have never been to a kirtan before and are already worried about singing badly. The leader presses a key, the drone begins, and before any song to Krishna or Shiva, the first line goes out to someone else. An elephant-headed god, with a broken tusk and a sweet in one hand. The room sings it back. Why start there?
screen: `A RUG, A HARMONIUM, A DRUM.` → `THE DRONE BEGINS.` → `THE FIRST SONG GOES TO GANESHA.`

segments.voice: Kirtan is singing the names and glories of God together, often as call and response. The leader sings a line, the room sings it back. A repertoire is simply the songs a group knows by heart, the ones that can start without a songbook. For the next few days we'll build one, a song at a time, in roughly the order an evening might run. Some halls begin with Ganesha. Tradition honors him first before many beginnings: a wedding, a new house, a school year, a puja. He is called the remover of obstacles, and also the lord of them, the one who can place a block in the road or lift it. Tradition tells more than one story of why he goes first. In one, from the Shiva Purana, Shiva restores the boy to life with an elephant's head after a terrible quarrel, and then declares that he will be worshipped before every other god. A Hindi aarti to him begins: Jai Ganesha, Jai Ganesha, Jai Ganesha Deva. Victory to Ganesha, victory to the god. The next line names his family plainly: his mother is Parvati, his father is Mahadeva, the great god, Shiva. So the first song of the night is partly a family introduction. Notice what that does in the room. This evening doesn't begin with the hardest song. It begins by clearing the road. The nervous newcomer gets a simple line to repeat, sung slowly, and by the third time round, the line is in the room. In a kirtan, the first obstacle can be as small as opening your mouth.
screen: `KIRTAN: NAMES SUNG BACK AND FORTH.` · `A REPERTOIRE: SONGS KNOWN BY HEART.` · `GANESHA, HONORED FIRST.` · `HIS SONG CLEARS THE ROAD.` · then, large: `BEGIN BY CLEARING THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the shoulders drop. Bring to mind one thing you're about to begin, today or this week. A conversation, a piece of work, a trip. Name it quietly. Then name one thing that might block it: tiredness, worry, a person, a habit. Don't try to solve it. Just see the obstacle clearly and set it down in front of you. If you pray, you can say Ganesha's name once, softly, as some Hindus do before a beginning. If not, simply rest with the road in front of you. The bell holds the time.
Kirtan repertoire. The songs a group sings together by heart. Today, the song that often opens the night: Ganesha's.
Your line: the first obstacle is opening your mouth. Today, before you start one task, pause long enough to name what might get in its way. Day nine hundred eighty-seven.
